findings.title: Dead helper `_create_process_for_shard` is never called
findings.body: The method `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shard(shard)` (lines 127-132) is defined but has no callers. The only restart path is in `_ensure_processes_alive`, which invokes `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. The single-shard helper is dead code and should either be removed or wired into the restart path so callers can target a specific shard.

findings.title: Docstring claims one process per shard, but processes shard subsets
findings.body: The class docstring (line 32) says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' That is no longer true: `__init__` actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and groups shards via `i % num_processes`. With `flusher_processes=2` and 4 shards, the docstring is misleading and the round-robin assignment also has performance implications (e.g., adjacent shards can end up in different processes and cross shard/processes). The docstring should describe the actual grouping behavior.

findings.title: CLI help for `--flusher-processes` is misleading
findings.body: `help="Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1."` implies that passing e.g. `--flusher-processes 8` always gives 8 processes. In reality `SpanFlusher.__init__` clamps via `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))`, and the help also describes the CLI default of 1 rather than the SpanFlusher default of `len(assigned_shards)`. If a user passes a value greater than the number of assigned partitions, they will silently get fewer processes than expected. The help should note the cap.

findings.title: `flusher_processes=0` is silently coerced to `len(assigned_shards)`
findings.body: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats 0 as falsy and falls back to one process per shard. An operator passing `--flusher-processes 0` likely expects 'no flusher' or an error, not a default-override that spawns more processes than they asked for. Use an explicit `None` check instead of `or`, or document/validate that 0 is not accepted.

findings.title: `test_flusher_processes_limit` never submits a message
findings.body: The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2` and that 4 shards are present in `process_to_shards_map`. It does not submit a payload, does not advance drift, and does not assert that any segment reaches the `produce_to_pipe`. The whole point of the multiprocess refactor is that shards split across processes are still flushed end-to-end; this test will silently pass even if the new `_create_process_for_shards` does not correctly wire shards to buffers or if the threading path is broken. Add at least one submit + flush assertion that exercises the cross-process flusher wiring.

findings.title: `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op due to the monkeypatch above it
findings.body: Lines 15-16 monkeypatch `time.sleep` to a no-op (`lambda _: None`). The comment on line 61 then says 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' and calls `time.sleep(0.1)`, but that call is also a no-op. The comment is misleading; the test passes only because the flusher thread likewise runs `time.sleep` as a no-op and busy-loops. Either drop the call/comment, or un-monkeypatch `time.sleep` for that single line so the intent matches the code.

findings.title: `if not process:` guard in `_ensure_processes_alive` is dead
findings.body: `self.processes` is populated in `_create_process_for_shards` and never has `None` values, so `if not process: continue` (line 222) is unreachable. Either remove the check or, if the intent was to skip dead slots, document why None entries would ever appear (e.g., a future graceful-shutdown slot).

findings.title: Per-submit Redis memory probe now scales with process count
findings.body: Original code did one `self.buffer.get_memory_info()` call per submit. New code iterates `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())`, so the consumer issues N Redis probes per submit where N equals the number of flusher processes (up to one per shard). Even though `submit` is described as not hot, on every call we now do N network round-trips to gather data that conceptually represents the same underlying Redis memory. Consider caching or aggregating memory info once per flush cycle instead of once per submit.

findings.title: `process.kill()` followed by immediate respawn can produce duplicate flushes
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, the unhealthy process is `kill()`-ed (non-blocking) and `_create_process_for_shards` is invoked immediately. The old subprocess may still be alive for some time (kill delivery, Redis I/O in flight), during which both the old and new flusher processes can independently call `buffer.flush_segments` and `producer.produce` on the same shard. That can produce duplicate `BUFFERED_SEGMENTS` messages on Kafka. The original code had a similar race but only one flusher existed; now that shards are shared across processes, the blast radius is wider. Consider `process.join(timeout)` before respawn, or use `terminate()` plus a join so the previous process truly exits first.

findings.title: `process_restarts` threshold allows one more restart than the constant suggests
findings.body: The check is `if self.process_restarts[process_index] > MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`, followed by increment + respawn. Tracing the counter: it starts at 0, is checked then incremented. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` the counter reaches 11 before `11 > 10` triggers, so the consumer actually restarts the process 11 times before raising, not 10. This is an off-by-one that pre-dates this PR, but it is worth aligning either the constant (to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS - 1`) or the comparison (`>= MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS`) so the cap matches the name.
